title: Heat a room with an open fireplace
summary: An open fireplace sends most of its heat up the chimney and can pull more warm air out of the house than it gives back, but small hot fires, a closed-off room and people sitting in the glow still make a room liveable. Check the chimney first, keep the damper open until the fire is completely out, because glowing coals make carbon monoxide, and keep a fire watch.

materials.qty: a day's supply indoors, the rest outside

materials.item: Fire screen that covers the whole opening
ABC fire extinguisher and chimney-fire suppressant sticks

steps.text: Check the chimney before the first fire, above all after years of disuse: nests and debris, cracks and soot or tar are what AD J lists, and an old damper plate can be brittle or stuck (AD J, MU G1735). See [Check a chimney](#guides/test_chimney).
Put a CO alarm and a smoke alarm in the room and an extinguisher near the fireplace (NRCan wood heating).
Close the room off: doors shut, bedding or heavy drapes over the doorways (MU GH5118). Keep a door and an opening window clear as ways out.
Open the damper fully before you light anything (CPSC 611, Pleasant Hearth doors). If the chimney is cold and smoke rolls into the room, crack a window for a few minutes (Drolet Part 1).
Set the grate close to the back wall (Pleasant Hearth doors) and light a small fire with newspaper and dry kindling (NRCan wood heating).
steps.warn: Never gasoline, kerosene or charcoal starter (NRCan wood heating).

steps.text: Keep it small and hot: feed it a few split pieces often and never let it smoulder or overload it (NRCan wood heating). A smouldering fire can leave the house colder than no fire (EPA AP-42).
Keep the screen closed, anything that burns at least 1 m (3 ft) from the front, and children and pets back (Pleasant Hearth doors).
steps.warn: Glass doors stay open while it burns unless their maker says otherwise: closed on a fire, tempered glass can overheat and shatter (Pleasant Hearth doors). Cold water on hot door glass can shatter it too.

steps.text: Sit and work in the fire's glow: it heats what it shines on (EPA AP-42). Babies, very old people, anyone drunk or sedated and anyone with numb feet can't always tell or move away from radiant heat, so seat them back where the glow is mild. Beds stay at least as far back as anything else that burns, 1 m (3 ft) from the front or more (Pleasant Hearth doors), and one person stays awake on fire watch while it burns (MU GH5118).
Stop adding wood well before bed and let it burn down to ash.
steps.warn: The damper stays fully open until the fire is completely out and the ashes are cold: glowing coals keep making carbon monoxide (Calgary fireplaces, CMHC wood heat).

steps.text: Next day, once the ashes are cold all the way through (stir them: they can hold live embers for days, Drolet Part 1), take them out in a lidded metal can and leave it outside, on the ground or concrete and never on a wooden deck, well away from anything that burns (Drolet Part 1).
Only now close the damper and any glass doors, to stop warm air going up the chimney (Calgary fireplaces, NRCan wood heating).
If an insert or a wood stove turns up, put it in only with a stainless liner running to the top of the chimney (NRCan wood heating). See [Install a wood stove](#guides/build_stove_install).

notes:
## What an open fireplace really gives you
- Most traditional open fireplaces lose over 90% of the fire's heat up the chimney (EPA fireplaces).
- They pull a lot of warm air out of the house while giving little heat back; in cold weather the efficiency can be near or below zero (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat).
- What you do get is radiant heat: the fire warms what it shines on. Some of that goes into warming the cold air pulled in to replace what went up the chimney, and a smouldering fire draws air without giving much radiant heat, so it can leave the house colder than no fire (EPA AP-42).
- Their big air appetite, poor burning and changeable draft make them more likely than other wood heaters to spill smoke into the room (NRCan wood heating).

So the way to use one is small, hot, bright fires, people sitting in the glow, and the warm air kept in one room. See [Get through winter in one heated room](#guides/skill_staying_warm) for choosing and closing off the room.

## What helps and what doesn't
| Measure | Does it help? | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Small, hot fire, fed often, never smouldering, not overloaded | Yes: the main thing you control | NRCan wood heating, EPA AP-42 |
| Grate close to the back wall of the firebox | Keeps the fire back from the opening; the door maker's rule | Pleasant Hearth doors |
| Closing the room off from the rest of the house | Keeps the heat you get in one place | MU GH5118 |
| A cast-iron fireback stood against the back wall | Protects the bricks and reflects some heat back into the room | NPS firebacks |
| Glass doors | Not while it burns: tempered glass blocks much of the radiant heat, and one door maker's manual says never close them on a fire. Closed when the fire is out, they cut the draft up the chimney | NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat, Pleasant Hearth doors |
| Tubular "heat-exchanger" grates and firebox liners | Only a minor gain, and used constantly they can dangerously overheat the area round the fireplace | NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat |
| Duct bringing outside air to the firebox | Unlikely to help; wind can reverse it and send hot exhaust through the duct | NRCan wood heating |
| Wax-and-sawdust fire logs | Less smoke, not more heat | NRCan wood heating |
| An insert or hearth-mount stove on a full liner | The real fix: nearly as efficient as a free-standing stove | NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat |

## The room
Pick the room with the fireplace, keep its doors shut and hang bedding or heavy drapes over the doorways (MU GH5118). Keep your way out: a door and a window that opens, both clear of snow ([Staying warm](#guides/skill_staying_warm)). The fire needs air: if smoke rolls out of the opening, something is starving it or fighting it, such as a range hood or bathroom fan running, or a cold chimney (NRCan wood heating, Drolet Part 1); Drolet's fix for a cold chimney is to crack a window for a few minutes when lighting (Drolet Part 1).

Keep things that burn at least 1 m (3 ft) from the front of the fireplace, keep children and pets well back (Calgary's 1 m from hot glass is its advice for gas fireplaces), and keep a screen that covers the whole opening closed except when you add wood: a closed screen is the barrier for sparks (Pleasant Hearth doors, Calgary fireplaces). Beds go further back than that. While it burns, someone stays awake on fire watch; drowsiness is a sign of carbon monoxide (MU GH5118).

## The first fire after years
Assume something has moved in or fallen down. Flues get blocked by nests and debris, and the exposed top decays first (AD J); a damper plate can be brittle from years of heat (MU G1735), and an old one may be stuck. Do the checks in [Check a chimney](#guides/test_chimney) first, and check the damper opens before every fire (CPSC 611). Then a small fire, with someone watching the chimney breast, the attic and the roof for smoke.

## Embers, the damper and carbon monoxide
A bed of glowing charcoal makes carbon monoxide even with no smoke or flame, so its exhaust must go completely outside (CMHC wood heat, NRCan wood heating). That means:
- **The damper stays fully open until the fire is completely out and the ashes are cold** (Calgary fireplaces). Closing it "to keep the heat in" over glowing coals sends the CO into the room.
- Plan the evening so the fire burns down to ash before you need to close up: stop adding wood well before bed.
- Ashes hold live embers for days and keep giving off CO: take them out in a lidded metal can and leave it outside on the ground or a non-combustible floor, away from anything that burns (Drolet Part 1).
- A working CO alarm in the room; know what it can and can't tell you: [Carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide).

## What not to put in it
- No gasoline, kerosene or charcoal starter to get it going (NRCan wood heating, Pleasant Hearth doors).
- No wrapping paper or loads of paper: they can flare into a flash fire (CPSC 611).
- No evergreen boughs or Christmas trees: dry greens burn like tinder, flare out of control and throw sparks into the room or up the chimney onto creosote (CPSC 611).
- It is not an incinerator for trash (Pleasant Hearth doors). See [What to burn](#guides/reference_what_to_burn).

## An insert or a stove, if one turns up
A fireplace insert is a wood stove made to sit in the fireplace opening; a hearth-mount stove sits on the hearth in front. Either one must vent through a stainless liner running all the way from its flue collar to the top of the chimney (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat). Older installs that let the exhaust find its own way up the big masonry flue burned badly and made a lot of creosote (NRCan wood heating). The fireplace and chimney must be cleaned of all deposits first (NRCan wood heating). A factory-built metal fireplace takes only an insert certified for it, and no wood stove ever goes on an air-cooled fireplace chimney (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat). For the stove itself see [Check a found wood stove](#guides/repair_wood_stove) and [Install a wood stove](#guides/build_stove_install).

## If the chimney catches fire
A roar or rumble, lots of smoke, flames from the top: get everyone out and follow [Sweeping and chimney fires](#guides/skill_chimney_sweeping). An open fireplace has no door to shut. The article names one suppressant pack, Kidde's FireEx, as usable in fireplaces as well as stoves, and says the maker advises covering the opening with fire-retardant material to cut the draft (FireRescue1). Keep some beside it.
